forces: Chorus and orchestra with trumpets and timpani
performers: London Symphony Orchestra; London Philharmonic Choir; Hermann Scherchen, conductor; Frederick Jackson, chorus master
intro: The “Hallelujah” chorus closes Part II of Handel’s Messiah, HWV 56. Hermann Scherchen conducts the London Symphony Orchestra and London Philharmonic Choir.

sections.label: A · Hallelujah in D major
sections.mNote: The strings play the theme; the choir follows.

sections.label: B · Tune in the basses
sections.mNote: “For the Lord” passes between the voices

sections.label: C · “King of kings”: long notes, choral replies
sections.mNote: Long held upper notes above quick replies from the other voices.

sections.label: D · “And he shall reign”: fugue subject returns
sections.mNote: The basses bring back the leaping fugue subject.

sections.label: A′ · Final Hallelujah
sections.mNote: A pause, then the final cadence from G to D.

cues.title: Opening, first violins and choir
cues.text: The first violins open with the rhythm of “Hallelujah”. Three bars later the choir enters on the word, all four parts together. The key is D major, with short choral cries and brief answering runs in the strings.
cues.evidence: Handel, Messiah, Hallelujah, bars 1–7; Joshua Koo’s Mutopia full score, violin and choral parts. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: “The kingdom of this world”, bars 33–41
cues.text: The quick cries stop. “The kingdom of this world” moves in measured crotchets, the choir singing together over a descending bass. At “the kingdom of our Lord” the phrase rises.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 33–41: choral setting of “The kingdom of this world” and “the kingdom of our Lord”. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Fugue on “And he shall reign”
cues.text: The basses begin “And he shall reign” with a subject that leaps up and down through the chord. Tenors, altos and sopranos then enter in turn. Short “Hallelujah” cries recur around the subject.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 41–51: bass entry in bar 41, tenor in 43, alto in 46 and soprano in 48. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: “King of kings”, sopranos and altos
cues.text: “King of kings” begins on a held A in the sopranos and altos. The sopranos then rise through D, E, F♯ and G, holding each note over faster entries in the other voices.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 51–68: sustained A in soprano and alto, followed by the soprano’s ascending proclamations. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Request to the audience, Dublin, 1742
cues.text: On 13 April 1742, the day of the first Messiah, the Dublin papers printed a request to the audience at the Music Hall in Fishamble Street. Ladies were asked “not to come with hoops” and gentlemen to come without their swords. This let more people fit into the hall, which benefited the charity.
cues.evidence: Dublin newspaper notices of 9 and 13 April 1742, transcribed in the Handel Reference Database, 1742 documents (the Stewards of the Charitable Musical Society’s request on the day of the performance): https://web.stanford.edu/~ichriss/HRD/1742.htm

cues.title: Final plagal cadence, bars 92–94
cues.text: The repeated “Hallelujah” cries break off. After a rest the choir sings the word once more in broad note values. The bass moves from G to D beneath it, and Handel places a fermata over the final D major chord.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 92–94: rest, final declaration, G-to-D plagal cadence and fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The basses take “For the Lord”
transitions.how: The basses take “For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth” on D, rising through E and F♯. The first violins double the tune low in their range, and the sopranos rest. The four-part writing of the opening divides into this melody and shorter “Hallelujah” answers in the other voices.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 17–24: bass and first-violin statement of “For the Lord”, followed by the upper voices. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459

transitions.title: Upper voices hold A over replies
transitions.to: C · “King of kings”: long notes, choral replies
transitions.how: In bars 49–56 the fugue cadences in A major. Sopranos and altos hold A for “King of kings”, tied across the barline. Tenors and basses reply with short “Hallelujah” figures, and the strings double these replies under the sustained upper-voice note.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 49–56: cadence in A major and sustained upper-voice proclamations over short replies. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459

transitions.title: The basses reopen the fugue
transitions.from: C · “King of kings”: long notes, choral replies
transitions.to: D · “And he shall reign”: fugue subject returns
transitions.how: The sopranos end their held high G and descend towards E as the harmony arrives on A major. In bar 69 the basses bring back “And he shall reign”, and the other voices take up the leaping theme again. The first violins join the sopranos’ entry.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 67–74: end of the sustained soprano G, A-major arrival and renewed bass fugue entry in bar 69. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459

transitions.title: Rest and final plagal cadence
transitions.from: D · “And he shall reign”: fugue subject returns
transitions.how: In bars 90–94, choir and orchestra interrupt their repeated “Hallelujah” figures with a rest. The last statement begins in longer notes, and the bass moves from G to D for the plagal cadence. All four voices finish together on the D major chord, held under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 90–94: repeated acclamations, rest and the final G-to-D cadence. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459

source.title: Handel, Messiah, HWV 56, Hallelujah, full score (Joshua Koo, Mutopia)
source.locator: Joshua Koo’s Mutopia full score and orchestral parts, bars 1–94. The choir begins in bar 4; trumpets and timpani first enter late in bar 14. The closing bars contain the rest, G-to-D cadence and final fermata.

timeline.note: First violins play the Hallelujah rhythm above the bass; trumpets and timpani rest.
The choir sings the word Hallelujah, with oboes doubling and strings answering.
Trumpets and timpani join the short Hallelujah replies.
The kingdom of this world moves in choral crotchets above a descending bass; brass and timpani rest.
Sopranos and altos hold A for King of kings; strings, brass and drums join the short answers below.
The high soprano and trumpet G descend towards E; the basses bring back And he shall reign.
Choir and orchestra pause before the last Hallelujah and its G-to-D cadence.

composer.epithet: Composer who filled London theatres with Italian opera and later put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg had a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant, and Prince Ruspoli provided him with singers and instrumentalists to write for. In the Dixit Dominus of 1707, a setting of a Latin psalm, five choral parts move at speed, then some voices hold dissonant notes while the others move underneath. He wrote chamber cantatas for a single singer. In Corelli’s Rome he learned to write for violin alongside the voice.
